en: Everyone who observed him
Called Sarybay a swine.
Born where no people saw him,
He cast the world into turmoil.
His valor was unlike all others;
The sly wretch brought dreadful calamity.
All the people grieved,
Despairing of their precious lives;
The whole nation mourned,
Despairing of its very existence.
If the moon grew dark and veiled,
Though no clouds covered the world,
“What would become of the sun?” they said.
“How will the encampment
Of the poor, few Kyrgyz settle?
What recourse will they have?” they said.
Külchoro’s winged steed—
From time immemorial,
Whenever Almambet’s son Külchoro
Rode forth into battle,
It sighted the foe from afar.
A beast that had campaigned against the khagan,
And brought down mighty khans,
It had grown accustomed to war.
It had a flowing tail and mane,
A magnificent creature indeed.
It leaped like a flea,
And grew sleek as a gun barrel.
It never panicked at the battle cry;
Even on a moonless watch,
It never misplaced a single step.
Its ears shone like lighted lamps,
Its hooves were broad as bowls.
If an enemy deliberately thrust a spear,
It darted aside to right or left.
From every mortal danger
It whisked the warrior away.
It was the winged steed beneath him.
Entering battle, it brought good fortune—
Such was Külchoro’s way.
Would he retreat before death?
His opponent was Sarybay;
Would he ever turn back from combat?
For the infidel son of an ogre
The end of time had come.
His spirit seethed beyond restraint,
And he staked everything upon fate.
His adversary was Sarybay,
A fearsome calamity such as this.
He had seen heroes of countless kinds,
And champions throughout the world,
Yet before his fated death
He had never seen upon the earth
Such a dreadful battle,
Nor a wrestler like this.
Against the infidel son of an ogre—
“Let me shed my blood for the people.
For my people and my nation,
Let me spill my precious blood;
Let me grapple with him and see.
Ever since I became Külchoro,
Ever since Külchoro mounted a horse,
I have seen giants of countless kinds
And endured the horrors of many battles,
Yet fate has never brought my death.
Never have I seen so fierce a champion,
So venomously strong as this infidel.
Long ago, God above,
My father Almambet’s pursuit,
His birth from Aruuke,
That poor soul’s tottering steps,
And all the hardships he endured;
How both my mother and father died,
Leaving me an orphan;
How I grew up an orphan,
And somehow joined my people;
How I matured and became a man,
And stood equal with heroes’ sons;
How I climbed awkwardly onto a horse,
And lived among men.
My doom has not come, and I have not died;
In all my life, never have I seen
Such a terrible calamity.
First, God created me;
You gave me life and made me a hero,
Made me a champion throughout the world.
Yet, O one God, you have made what remains of me
Equal to the black earth.
You did not hear my prayer or my words;
He was about to break my back.
He ruined my stronghold
And cast my people into turmoil.
He dug my grave deep
And showed us a marvel.
The end of time has now begun;
Nowhere in the world have I seen
Such anguish and grief—
A calamity fallen upon the people,” he said,
As the nation wailed in sorrow.
“He truly is a hero and a champion;
Sarybay, the ogre’s son,
Who brought the whole world under his sway,
Is the mightiest man on earth.
He tears apart all who encounter him;
He is like a raging boar.
Finding no mountain to strike,
And no enemy to fight,
This brute has come here.
His monstrous cruelty is plain;
The warriors despair of their lives,
And the people stand wailing:
“What inheritance could I gain
By making these people wail?
For this land protected by Kydyr,
I shall attack the raging brute
And go to my sacrifice.
His valor is as vast as a mountain;
Let no one say that Külchoro
Gave his people and nation up as plunder.
Let the khan I grapple with die;
If my own dear eyes close,
Let all the people of this great realm die with me.
Against the infidel hero Sarybay,
Now I shall thrust my spear.
For my poor, beloved people,
I shall sacrifice this life!
While this devoted warrior still stands,
How could I surrender my people?
Sarybay has run wild;
I shall match this fellow’s prancing
And see what comes of it!
If angered, I shall take him;
Or against this emboldened infidel,
I shall die this very moment.
Thus, filled with fury,
I shall grapple with him and see.”
“When we gained countless riches,
When we raided the land of Künjüt,
And stretched the black-steel Zulfiqar
Toward the enemy,
When in every place where we traded blows
Our strength proved equal,
Why did I not die then?
Who did not jauntily wear
A blue-lynx coat and black fur cap?
While fortune crowned one’s head,
Who did not stride about roaring?
When they beheld our precious lives,
Did not the worlds tremble?
We brought misery upon the world;
Were we not lions, were we not khans?
Throughout the eighteen thousand worlds,
None remained who dared swing a lasso at us.
When we roared in anger,
The whole world plunged into turmoil.
When we scowled in wrath,
Your eighteen thousand worlds
Were utterly laid waste.
Now there is no valor, no heroism;
Against the infidel son of an ogre,
Our former courage is gone.
Has God stricken our strength?
Before the infidel son of an ogre,
Has God condemned us to disgrace?
Our heroism once surged and thundered,
Once it seems to have surpassed all bounds.
Perhaps mighty God and Kydyr decreed
That before this raging infidel
We should be humiliated.
My heart burns, my liver is aflame;
When glory flees from everyone,
Is this what the worthless world becomes?
When I was born,
You had ninety beasts slaughtered for my feast.
You bade them range across the whole world
And slaughter them as they went.
Yet now a warrior such as this
Is about to destroy my mullah
And, I fear, carry away as plunder
My golden-throned palace!
Long ago, the one God above
Made me a champion who shook the age.
Without making me equal to a single infidel,
Why have you diminished me so greatly?
Yesterday, on the plain of Jylgyndy,
Along the broad Talas,
When we shot deer if we grew bored,
And, when tireless in former days,
Played freely at our ease;
When the black-steel Zulfiqar
Was kept gleaming with oil;
When we drove
The black Chinese and Manchu before us;
Why did death not come then,
As we thrust our spears and broke their ranks?
Why did no bullet strike me dead?
When the Kyrgyz sprawled at ease
Across Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
We went and conquered Afghanistan—
Whoever met us there escaped unharmed?
With unsheathed swords in hand,
We slaughtered the Chinese,
Making them scream,
And drove them all the way to Beijing.
When we forced those mighty armored men
Back inside Beijing,
When there was more gold and silver
Than we could load and carry,
And more beautiful noble brides
Than we could seize as booty,
When we besieged Kara-Shaar and Kambil,
Holding them trapped,
And beat down
The black Khitans and Manchus,
Why did I not die then?
There were pounds of coin and yellow gold—
Where are the days of old?
Will a day ever come
When we defeat this infidel son of an ogre?
Like a dark falcon of prey,
Will a day come when we swoop upon him?
Will there be a day when we deliver
His rightful punishment into his own hands?”
So saying, Külchoro
Loaded his ornate musket.
The lion born a peerless champion
Lamented the days gone by.
Combat had exhausted him;
He was pressed into dreadful straits.
His true humiliation became clear,
And he despaired of his fly-like life.
A terrible fury seized him;
He simply bound
His precious life upon a hair.
Heedless of high or low,
Never thinking he might die,
Looking at nothing around him,
He spared not his life at all
Against the Heaven-stricken swine.
He yearned to die
And to give the infidel ogre’s son
The punishment he truly deserved.
Külchoro, son of Almambet—
The warrior whose fortune was complete,
The hero supported by the spirits.
His wrestling strength was extraordinary,
His valor beyond measure.
When his fit of rage seized him,
He ranged across the vast steppe.
Whoever provoked his wrath,
He caught in his fangs and chewed,
Then drove beneath his feet.
Throughout the eighteen thousand worlds,
None remained who dared swing a lasso at him.
No enemy dared confront him,
And none prevailed against him in contest.
